You can't really prosecute a sitting President because of the sovereign immunity doctrine. Essentially, the government can't do anything "illegal" because it determines what's legal and illegal. Certainly the Department of Justice would have a difficult time indicting or prosecuting a sitting President so while serving under the President, and even a special prosecutor would have to focus mostly on impeachment.

The key is removing the sovereign immunity, which can only be done through impeachment in Congress. The House brings the charges and the Senate tries the case. A President who is duly impeached, convicted, and removed from office is then subject to criminal prosecution for any crimes committed in office. The closest we ever came to this was the Nixon resignation (not an impeachment although it very nearly could have been), and he was pardoned by his successor, Gerald Ford. We would almost certainly see something similar in a future case unless the crime were particularly egregious and the evidence particularly clear-cut.

If you're interested in more details, here is a lengthy examination from the Justice Department: A Sitting President's Amenability to Indictment and Criminal Prosecution
